Q: Scannerless Parser Generators A:

I have written a 'scan-on-demand' parser. It is a kind of compromise between a parser with a scanner and a scanner-less parser.

It allows for 'no reserved key-words', and enables one language to be embedded/nested in another.

A good example of this nesting is the Dot grammar from graphviz https://graphviz.gitlab.io/, where XML/HTML can be embedded in the outer graph language.

You can see a demo of my parser and the Dot grammar at https://info.itemis.com/demo/agl/editor

and more details on the parser can be found here https://medium.com/@dr.david.h.akehurst/a-kotlin-multi-platform-parser-usable-from-a-jvm-or-javascript-59e870832a79

Q: Optimizing Column Selection for Row-Wise Minimum Sum in Matrices A:

This problem is essentially equivalent to the k-median problem: Given a set of m Facilities F and n Customers, select k facilities such that the sum of distances from the customers to the respective closest of the k facilities is minimized. Why is there an equivalence? You can define a m x n distance Matrix D where D_{i,j} is the distance from Customer i to Facility j. Then, selecting k Columns corresponds to selecting k Facilities, and the minimization of the sum of row-wise minima corresponds to minimizing the sum of distances from the customers to the respective closest of the k facilities. Conversely, you can regard the Matrix as the distance-Matrix. Note however, that some versions of the k-median problem assume the distances are a proper metric, which puts additional constraints on the cost-Matrix such as D_{i,j} >= 0, just to name one.

Also note that this is a very hard problem. It is not only NP-hard, which would be bad enough, but its also W[2]-hard with respect to k. If you don't know what that means, it is basically "Assuming a certain conjecture (the Exponential Time Hypothesis), it requires O(n^Θ(k)) (exponential) runtime to solve this problem", making it prohibitively expensive to solve it exactly (for moderately large inputs).

This problem has been studied extensively. There are many heuristic (inexact) algorithms which obtain good solutions for most practical applications. For example, a simple greedy algorithm would start with no column, and iteratively add the column which decreases the total sum by the most amount. Unfortunately, this algorithm has no approximation guarantee, meaning that for some instances, the ratio between the optimum sum and the sum of the solution by the greedy algorithm may be arbitrarily large.

Another inexact algorithm starts with any set of columns (for example the set computed by the greedy algorithm) and checks if the sum can be improved by swapping a column for some other column. It makes these swaps until no swap improves the sum. Again, this algorithm provides high quality solutions for most real-world instances. Additionally, it even gives an approximation guarantee if we assume metric distances, namely the sum for the solution after the algorithm is done is never higher than 5 times the smallest possible sum - that doesn't sound great, but you'd need some specially engineered "bad" instances for this algorithm to actually perform this poorly. For most cases, its a great choice.

If there is really no way around computing the globally optimum solution, then I'd recommend looking into ILP-solvers. They usually still handle instances with n,m ≈ 1000 "well".

Q: Overcome non-linear constraints with new design? A:

It's possible I'm misreading your description, but I think you are saying that you want no losses "for each product at each store" using your profit function.

If so, that can be encoded without any binary variables, which will keep the program linear and non-integer.

So when you say, "For each of X and each of Y " in programming, that usually is a nested loop. We loop over all the x values and for each of those, we loop over all the y values. The same basic concept applies here, but we need to keep track of the profit for each product and each store. To keep track of that, almost everything in your model needs to be double indexed to keep track of that. You have it mixed in a few spots in your example. We need to keep track of how many we deliver, sell, ship all by [shop, product]. Likely same for shipping cost unless that is insensitive to the store.

So, let's define:

purchase[s, p]   = quantity of product p purchased by store s, also the amount shipped to the store

sell[s, p]       = quantity of product p sold by store s (may be a variable or data??)

price[s, p]      = price of p at s

wholesale[s, p]  = wholesale price of p at s (may not be dependent on s...)

ship[s, p]       = cost to ship p to s

If that is agreed, your profit per item per store is:

P[s, p] = sell[s, p] x price[s, p] - purchase[s, p] x (wholesale[s, p] + ship[s, p])

That is the basis of your set of constraints, which will be a set of equations | S x P | in size. You just need to encode that "for each s and for each p " >= 0. That is it

Then for maximizing overall profit, it is a double sum over s & p

Q: serial communication using binary A:

I have been using NI Max to send basic serial commands, but in response to all queries, I seem to be getting gibberish.

That is not a clear description of what you have done nor what any response looks like.

Obviously this is a binary message scheme.
Rather than deal with binary values, most user interfaces use hexadecimal representation of those values.
But the default mode for terminal-emulation programs is text, i.e. the binary value of each received serial frame is converted/displayed as a character per ASCII or UTF-8 codes.

So you probably want to instead use the terminal-emulation program in a numeric rather than a text mode for both input (from keyboard) and output (on the display). But this may be a capability that only some terminal-emulation programs have.
